hints: Focus on counting all the valence electrons in CO and seeing where they must go if C and O are already triple bonded.
Notice that oxygen starts with six outer electrons but carbon starts with only four, so think about who must donate to make the third bond.
Remember what a triple bond is always made of in terms of sigma and pi, then add up the leftover lone pairs on C and on O.
walkthrough:
**Count the total outer electrons**

Think of CO like a puzzle with 10 outer electrons to place. Carbon brings 4 and oxygen brings 6.

$$\text{total valence electrons} = 4 + 6 = 10$$

**Build the triple bond with a dative bond**

A normal shared triple bond would leave carbon short. So oxygen donates one of its lone pairs to carbon to make the third bond.

$$:C \equiv O: \text{ where one bond is } O \rightarrow C$$

**Check lone pairs and pi bonds**

After using 6 electrons for the triple bond, 4 electrons remain. That is one lone pair on carbon and one lone pair on oxygen, so two lone pairs in total.

$$10 - 6 = 4 \text{ electrons} = 2 \text{ lone pairs}$$

**Split the triple bond into sigma and pi**

Every triple bond is always one sigma plus two pi bonds. So CO must contain two $\pi$ bonds.

$$\text{triple bond} = 1\sigma + 2\pi$$

**Conclude all three statements**

We have two lone pairs, a dative bond from O to C, and two pi bonds. That means 1, 2 and 3 are all correct.

options.A: Correct because all three statements are true. CO has one lone pair on C and one on O, one of the three bonds is dative from O to C, and a triple bond contains two pi bonds.
options.B: Incorrect because it leaves out statement 3. Many students accept the lone pairs and dative bond but forget that a triple bond is 1 sigma + 2 pi, so two pi bonds must be present.
options.C: Incorrect because it leaves out statement 1. Students sometimes think all electrons are used in the triple bond, but counting 10 valence electrons leaves 4 electrons as two lone pairs.
options.D: Incorrect because it includes only statement 1. This comes from drawing CO as $C=O$ with extra lone pairs and missing the unusual triple bond with dative character.
